newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean minister, more MPs target of Hanbo probe.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean minister, more MPs target of Hanbo probe.

text.p: South Korean prosecutors summoned a cabinet minister and more members of parliament on Wednesday in a widening probe into a loan scandal, but criticism lingered that only the tip of a sleazy iceberg had been revealed.

Senior prosecutor Choi Byung-koog told reporters Home Affairs Minister Kim Woo-suk and two lawmakers would be questioned on Wednesday on suspicion of taking kickbacks in connection with loans to the failed Hanbo Steel Co.
"They will be investigated as suspects," Choi said.

The lawmakers are Hwang Byung-tai, a former ambassador to China and now the head of the Finance and Economy Committee at the National Assembly, and Kwon Roh-kap, a top aide to main opposition leader Kim Dae-jung.

Hwang and the minister are also close associates of President Kim Young-sam, who last month ordered a thorough probe into five trillion won ($5.8 billion) of loans Hanbo Steel racked up before it was declared insolvent on January 23.

On Tuesday, prosecutors arrested two ruling party lawmakers -- one another close associate of Kim Young-sam and the other the highest ranking official in the ruling New Korea Party after the president and the party chairman.
They were the first politicians to be arrested over the loan scandal that has shocked South Koreans and put the heat on Kim Young-sam in a presidential election year.
President Kim has described the scandal as a typical example of corruption which is still widespread despite an anti-graft campaign he launched after taking office in 1993.
The anti-graft drive and his reputation have been tarnished in the past year following the arrest of several of his top officials, including a defence minister, on bribery charges.
Newspaper editorials and political analysts said the Hanbo probe had so far only touched the surface of the scandal.
"The investigation into the political circle touched only the outer branches of the Hanbo incident," the Hankook Ilbo newspaper said in an editorial.
It said the probe had not reached the "core" of the problem by identifying those fully responsible for pressuring bankers to offer the huge loans.
Hanbo Group founder Chung Tae-soo has already been arrested on charges of fraud and other violations over the scandal. Two bankers have also been arrested on bribery charges.
The two deputies already arrested -- Hong In-gil, former senior official at the presidential Blue House, and Chung Jae-chull -- have been charged with accepting Hanbo kickbacks.

The prosecution accused Hong of accepting 800 million won from the Hanbo tycoon who asked him to persuade banks to provide loans to the steelmaker, flagship of South Korea's 14th largest conglomerate. Chung was accused of taking 100 million won.
Hong told reporters before he was arrested that he was a "feather blown by wind".
"The Hanbo scandal has again highlighted the corrupt alliance between politics and business," an Asian diplomat said.
"Many South Koreans believe the prosecution has shed light on only the tip of a sleazy iceberg."
The local media has published new names of allegedly crooked politicians daily but all except opposition deputy Kwon have denied taking bribes.
Kwon said he had nothing to do with Hanbo loans, although he said had taken between 140 million and 160 million won from Hanbo, partly to fund an election campaign.

He said he also accepted a further 100 million won from the arrested ruling party lawmaker Chung, who prosecutors said passed on money from the tycoon in a bid to silence criticism over the huge loans that exceeded the value of their collateral.
Kwon said he did not know the money came from Hanbo.
